# Notes, Written Before an Announcement Date Exists

*Deliberately before. Once a date is on a slide, the transition stops being a design problem and becomes a countdown, and everything after that is defence of the countdown. The competitor who lost a fifth of its base almost certainly had a very good date.*

---

## What we think we're treating

"Investors discount lumpy revenue" is doing a lot of work in the brief, and it hides three different ailments that take different medicine.

**A disclosure problem.** Underneath the lumpy licence line there is almost certainly a large, boring, highly durable maintenance stream that we have never presented as what it is. If we report one number that mixes a heroic quarter's licences with a utility annuity, the market prices the blend at the volatility of the worst component. Treatment: re-cut the reporting. No business model change required. This is the cheapest possible outcome and we should test it before spending three years and a fifth of the base to get the same multiple.

**A cadence problem.** Paid upgrades require us to manufacture a release large enough to justify an invoice. That distorts engineering into version-shaped lumps, starves continuous improvement, and trains customers to skip every other release and negotiate. Treatment: subscription — genuinely, and for the right reason. This is the honest case, and it's a product argument, not a finance one.

**A monetisation problem.** The base is priced by what it bought years ago rather than what it uses now, and there's no mechanism to capture growth in usage, seats, or data. Treatment: subscription, again, but the design brief is *expansion*, not *conversion*.

My suspicion: the disclosure problem is real and partially free, the cadence problem is the actual justification, and the monetisation problem is where the money is — while the transition will be planned and measured entirely as a conversion exercise, because conversion is the only one with a countable numerator.

One precondition, which nobody puts in these plans: **a subscription is a standing promise to keep improving. If engineering cannot ship continuously, we are not selling a subscription, we are selling rent.** Customers can tell the difference within four quarters and they take it very personally. Worth establishing quietly whether release engineering can actually hold the promise before finance builds a model on it.

---

## The trough is three numbers and only one of them hurts

Recognised revenue collapses. Billings dip much less if we insist on annual prepay. Cash may barely move at all, and free cash flow can *rise* in year two because deferred revenue is a lovely thing to carry.

So the first move is not a pricing decision. It's this: **change the scoreboard while the old numbers still look good.** Introduce ARR, net revenue retention, billings, RPO and subscription mix as reported, guided metrics two to four quarters *before* anything transitions. Metrics introduced from strength are read as maturity. The identical metrics introduced in the first bad quarter are read as excuse-making, and once that reading takes hold it does not reverse.

A note on a temptation. Under current accounting, a multi-year on-premise term licence can often be recognised largely at delivery, which makes the trough look shallow and buys a year of peace. It is available, it works, and it stores up a comparison problem that will detonate later at a worse moment. If we use it, we disclose the amount explicitly every quarter and guide ex-it. Optics purchased in secret get repriced with interest.

---

## The offer, and the one thing we never touch

The abrupt switch fails for a specific reason: it converts a commercial change into a property dispute. People who bought a perpetual licence believe they own something, because they do. Attack that and you don't get churn, you get an organised campaign, a third-party maintenance ecosystem, and a user group that becomes a press outlet.

So:

**Nobody loses anything.** Existing perpetual licences remain live, permanently, at the version they're on. No sunset date, ever. Say it once, plainly, and then never mention it again. Almost no one will exercise the fallback; everyone needs it to exist. It is the cheapest insurance we will ever buy.

**Add a reactivation covenant.** Contractual undertaking that if we ever withdraw the subscription service, perpetual entitlement at the last delivered version revives automatically. Costs nothing. Removes the single fear that drives procurement teams to organise against us.

**Then make subscription a different product, not the same product on worse terms.** This is where most transitions are lazy. If subscription is "the thing you owned, but now you rent it," the customer is correctly insulted. It should carry what cannot exist perpetually: continuous delivery, hosted services, security commitments and patch SLAs, entitlement portability across environments, cross-product access, benchmarking data, whatever we have that only works when it's connected. **We're not asking them to give up ownership. We're asking them to buy something that ownership can't deliver.**

**Perpetual stays on the price list** — priced honestly, uplifted annually, and receiving maintenance but not new capability. We don't kill it. We let it become quaint. The customers who will never subscribe — air-gapped, regulated, sovereign, industrial — are a permanently profitable segment, and forcing them is how we manufacture the competitor's twenty per cent.

---

## Pricing, and choosing the depth of the hole

The trough's depth is a decision, and I'd rather it were deep and short than shallow and long. Two years is a strategy; four years is a narrative of management failure and an open invitation to an activist. Conversion pricing should be set to move the base fast.

The arithmetic that matters is the maintenance payer's delta, not the new-logo price. If maintenance runs around a fifth of licence value annually, subscription somewhere in the low-to-mid thirties of that value gives a three-year TCO that is roughly neutral against buying again and upgrading, and a five-year that is modestly worse — which is defensible only because the entitlement is materially larger. Close the gap with **bundled entitlement rather than discount**. Discount is permanent margin surrendered; entitlement is marginal-cost cheap and can be withdrawn from future cohorts.

Two mechanisms worth the complexity:

**A founder rate.** Convert within the first four quarters and the perpetual investment is credited as a permanent discount band that travels with the account. Not a promotional year-one price that expires — a rate they keep, which they will mention to their peers, which is the point. It also makes early conversion strictly better than late, which is how we avoid everyone waiting to see what we do next.

**Multi-year prepay, priced attractively.** Cash through the trough, RPO on the balance sheet, and it removes the account from the annual renegotiation cycle at precisely the moment we look weakest.

And the cheapest conversion is the one no human touches: a self-serve path priced better than any rep can offer, aimed at the long tail. Sales attention is our scarcest input and most of the base doesn't need it.

---

## Sales compensation, which is where this quietly dies

Reps aren't going to sabotage this out of malice. They'll do it rationally, by selling perpetual in the last three weeks of a quarter because their mortgage is annual and the transition is multi-year. The design must make the right behaviour the *individually* profitable one, not the corporately virtuous one.

- **Pay on ACV, with a transition multiplier.** For roughly eight quarters, subscription pays as though the deal were some multiple of its annual value — enough that a good rep's earnings curve is flat or better through the change. Fund it explicitly as a disclosed one-off transition cost. It is dramatically cheaper than replacing the top quartile of a sales force mid-transition, which is what the competitor probably also did and didn't put in the post-mortem.
- **Conversions pay, and pay well.** Nobody converts their own base for zero credit. For eight quarters, base conversion should be the most lucrative line on the plan, then decay on a published schedule so the cliff is expected rather than discovered.
- **Perpetual stays sellable and stops being worth selling.** Same deal, materially lower rate, and requiring an approval that takes a week. We don't ban it — bans produce creative misconduct. We make it tedious.
- **Twelve-month clawback on churn**, or we will buy a great deal of junk that leaves in year two, precisely when we need retention to be the whole story.
- **Resist the hunter/farmer split for now.** Continuity of ownership is what makes a converting customer feel handled rather than processed, and a handoff at the moment of conversion is a gift to a competitor's displacement team.
- **Move executive long-term incentives to ARR and net retention *before* the first converted deal.** If leadership is still paid on recognised revenue through the trough, the plan is decorative and everyone below can see it.

---

## Reading the competitor's fifth properly

Before we treat twenty per cent as a horror: a fifth of *what*? Logos or revenue? If it was the bottom quintile by spend and the top quintile by support burden, they may have improved the business and reported a disaster. Where did those customers go — to a live competitor, or to running an unsupported version forever, which is not churn so much as deferred re-acquisition? And how much of it was the forced sunset versus the fact that they raised price and removed the fallback in the same announcement?

Related, and more uncomfortable: **a portion of our installed base has already churned and hasn't told us.** Maintenance payers three or more releases behind are dead accounts still generating an invoice. Subscription will reveal them, and their loss will be booked in the trough and read as damage the transition caused. Count them now, publish the number to the board now, and take the write-down before we own it — otherwise it will be discovered in quarter five and re-labelled as a new problem.

---

## Keeping the board and the market in the room

**Publish the trough ourselves, and under-promise the floor.** One shape, one bottom, one exit date, guided conservatively enough that we beat it twice. The mechanism that ends these transitions early is not the trough — it's the second downward revision. That's when the board's nerve goes and the CEO is replaced by someone who fixes it by selling perpetual licences again.

**Disclose cohorts, not aspirations.** Conversion rate, uplift multiple, gross and net retention by conversion cohort, quarter after quarter. That's the evidence a long-horizon investor needs in order to underwrite the far side. Everything else is a story; cohorts are a machine you can watch working.

**Expect the shareholder register to turn over, and help it.** Some holders own us for the earnings and should sell — that's not a failure, it's hygiene. Meeting the buyers of recurring-revenue businesses starts six to twelve months before the first weak quarter, not during it.

**Buy back stock in the trough if the cash supports it,** which deferred revenue suggests it will. Nothing else states conviction as economically, and it also raises the price of the take-private that someone will otherwise propose to us at the bottom.

**And write down, while everyone is calm, the things we will not do to defend a quarter.** A cap on perpetual mega-deals. A cap on revenue pull-forward. No sunset threats to force conversion. Signed in month zero by people who will be under real pressure in quarter five, when a single large upfront deal would make the number and the argument for taking it will sound extremely reasonable.

---

## Sequence

Quarters −2 to 0: new metrics introduced from strength; dead-account write-down taken; executive LTI re-based; engineering cadence proved on one product line.

Quarters 1–4: founder rate open to the maintenance base; transition multiplier live in sales comp; self-serve path for the tail; perpetual quietly made tedious. Conversion cohorts published from the first quarter, however small.

Quarters 5–8: expansion pricing, which is where the actual value is and where everyone will have stopped looking; multiplier decays on schedule; buyback if the trough is behaving.

---

## The awkward possibility

That the endpoint isn't a full transition at all. That the right steady state is a permanent hybrid — perpetual for the segment that will never rent, subscription for everyone else — and that most of the multiple we're chasing was available from clearer disclosure and a genuinely continuous release cadence, without the trough, the comp upheaval, or the fifth of the base.

That would be an unwelcome finding for whoever has already told the board this is a transformation. Worth establishing early which we're being asked for.
